utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Baraybar. Welcome to the Tribunal. Will you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much and please sit down. Mr. Elderkin from the Prosecution has questions for you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon. As you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin, and I'll have a few questions for you. But first, please could you say your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My name is Jose Pablo Baraybar Do Carmo. I will spell that for the record, J-o-s-e P-a-b-l-o B-a-r-a-y-b-a-r D-o C-a-r-m-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I know that you have a binder of documents in front of you today. Could you tell the Court what is in that binder?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The binder contains my expert reports as well the previous court transcripts relating to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Everyone knows what you have in front of you, and if you need to look at that at any time, please just let us know. Can you say if you recall testifying here in the Popovic case in March of 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is there a correction which should be made in that testimony to your profession which is, in various places, referred to as forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it should read forensic anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. And noting this correction, does the transcript fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move at this stage for the admission of the witness's prior testimony as well as the previously admitted exhibits, and those have been, I think, already provisionally numbered in a memorandum. I can read out the numbers, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first one, the transcript of the testimony in the Popovic case will be received as P1048. The others, you should not read all the numbers but give us the first and the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the range is P1049 through P1070, and additionally one which is out of sequence, and that is P938. P938, just for Your Honours' reference, appears on the list between P1069 and 1070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was already marked for identification for another witness we haven't heard yet, I take. These documents will be received with the given numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And now with Your Honour's permission, I would like to read a short summary of the witness's evidence. Jose-Pablo Baraybar is a forensic anthropologist. He has previously testified before this Tribunal concerning Srebrenica in the Krstic and Popovic trials. He has worked on forensic investigations since 1991, including for the United Nations missions in Haiti and Kosovo, for the ICTR in Rwanda, and for the ICTY from 1996 to 2002. During his work for the ICTY, Mr. Baraybar worked on the exhumation and analysis of the remains of victims from Srebrenica. From 1997 onwards, Mr. Baraybar was the chief anthropologist at the mortuary which handled the remains recovered from graves. The role of the anthropologists at the mortuary was to determine the age, sex and stature of victims, to estimate the minimal number of individuals or MNI, based on the remains recovered, and to assist in reconstruction of broken parts, in order to determine the type of injury sustained by the victim. Mr. Baraybar also led teams of archeologists working in the field on Srebrenica-related exhumations in 1999 and 2001. Mr. Baraybar prepared a number of reports which set out the findings of the exhumations and which calculate the minimal number of individuals recovered from Srebrenica-related mass graves. According to Mr. Baraybar's calculations, the ICTY exhumed at least 2.541 separate individuals from Srebrenica-related primary and secondary graves between 1996 and 2001. That concludes my summary, Your Honours. And with your permission, I would like to ask a few additional questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move on, I have to note that we have a problem in the transcript in e-court with the page numbers. We have now page number 174, but I'm sure we haven't filled so many pages in LiveNote. The pages are correct, and if I compare them, that means 174 is the same as 4 in LiveNote. Please carry on, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, can we start by having you tell us a bit more about, first of all, your work at the ICTR and then moving on to how you came to the ICTY, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: ICTR created what was called, if I recall correctly, the scientific support unit to the Office of the Prosecutor. This unit was led by a medical doctor, Andrew Thompson, and had as its staff two anthropologists; one senior and one junior, me being the junior and Dr. Will Haglund being the senior, an engineer and a logistician. These units were the one that performed primarily two -- the investigation of two cases for the ICTR at the time, one of them led to the indictment of Clement Kayeshima, if I'm not mistaken, and the second one against Georges Anderson Rutaganda. By the end of the first semester of 1996, this unit was lent to ICTY. We were supposed to come to the Balkans, specifically to Bosnia, to conduct some exhumations for some six weeks. Obviously, the six weeks extended for much, much longer than that and became closer to six months. As a matter of fact, I do recall returning to Rwanda to actually collect my personal effects only one year after I left for six weeks. Only 1997 -- I became an employee of the Tribunal of ICTY as such. At the time I was still on loan, so to speak, from ICTR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think your ICTY history is covered in detail in your prior testimony, but just for the sake of record, could you give us a brief account of what you've been doing since you left the ICTY and when did you leave the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I left the ICTY in 2002, I believe about June. Then I became the head of the Office of Missing Persons and Forensics in the United Nations mission in Kosovo until 2007, I believe, May 1st, when I went back to my home country, Peru. There, I am the executive director of the Peruvian forensic anthropology team, a non-government organisation dealing with the issue of the missing as a consequence of the internal conflict in Peru. This organisation that I support also conducts a number of trainings in various parts of the world, including the Philippines, the Congo, Nepal and places of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Focusing on your work at the ICTY, as the chief forensic anthropologist at the mortuary in Bosnia, how would you describe your role?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The way to actually -- there were multiple tasks that I had conducted. Perhaps the most important one was to assemble the teams that would actually work with us in the mortuary and in the field for that matter, setting common protocols and forms to have some consistency on the recordings of the various things, and in addition working, doing case work, because I was not some type of supervisor that would just, like, sat and supervise people. I was also working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did the case work for you and the other anthropologists involve when you were at the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Let me answer in a bit of a narrative that would actually give a bigger picture of how the thing worked. The remains that we exhumed from the sites would arrive to the mortuary in body bags. These body bags will be scanned with a fluoroscope, that is some kind of an x-ray machine, to look for metal fragments, be it shrapnel bullets or live grenades, as in some cases we have encountered. The body then would be placed on the table, the autopsy table. Pictures would be taken, clothing would be separated from the remains. At the table, there would be a pathologist, an autopsy technician and an anthropologist, and then it would be a scene-of-crime officer that would be going from table to table, generally, collecting the various evidences. The anthropologist would be responsible then, and after agreeing with the pathologist, on removing parts for age and/or sex determination. Some occasions, the remains were badly decomposed and there were not external genitalia to be able to determine sex. And also reconstructing, after cleaning of course, any bone that was shown to be broken. As you know, bones in that context were broken by actions after the death of the people, in order to rob -- and I'm using a popular term -- robbed the graves in which an excavator, for example, would go through bodies and will fragment them, or people that have been actually been killed, been shot, or had injuries caused by projectiles or things of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, to have P00903 on the screen? That's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, you mentioned the task of reconstructing bone fragments. Could you describe what we are seeing now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You're seeing the left side of a skull -- of a human skull. If you look at it, the left side of the screen will be the face and the right side would be the back part, and you see some linear element, that would be the zygomatics, or cheeks of this person. Where the number 1 is, there is a round hole that is actually the entrance of a gunshot and all this fluffy white elements you see below the number 1 and on the right side of number 1, are actually the results of the glue we use to piece all these fragments together. So this skull that looks like a skull now was actually a co-mingled group of fragments that we have to put together like a jigsaw to understand what actually broke the skull, that, in this case, was a gunshot wound that you can see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could see now, please, P00910.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And again, with the image we are seeing, can you describe to us what it is and if there is any reconstruction work visible?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure. You have an femur, if I'm not mistaken, it's a right femur - although we should see in the vertical, we are now seeing it horizontally - and that's a leg bone, by the way, the thigh bone. So what you can see here is that these bones -- this bone has been fragmented perfect, has been fragmented into multiple -- multiple pieces. The arrow, the second arrow, from above to below, shows again another gunshot wound. And I will use this thing to indicate where it is, roughly here. Have I done anything? I cannot see any -- what should I press?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If it's possible, the usher could assist. Yes, please. Sorry, but I mean the circle should be slightly to the left. Anyway, in that area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You could delete your marking and you could do it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, how do I delete it? All right. Perfect. Okay. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I don't know if there is a technical way to change the colour of that marking, but I think green on green is going to be quite hard to see if this thing doesn't have the same resolution in future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. So that circle shows an area, the likely area of a gunshot wound. You can also see below and above that circle that there are some fractures, some fracture lines that are running above and below, and this is what is expected from such an injury. So in this case, again, this thigh bone was just comprised with many fragments that have been pieced together with this glue to show exactly what was the agent that caused the fracturing of the bone, and in this case it would be a gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In order for us to make a request to have this in evidence, I assume it would be helpful to have the witness's initials and perhaps the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is not necessary. We have the marking on the screen and if we receive it, and we will do that, it can be combined with our transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I move to have it admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With Exhibit P1305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I'd like to turn now to a different topic, which is that of the calculation of the minimal number of individuals. Can you tell us what MNI, minimal number of individuals, means and why was this method used to determine the numbers in Srebrenica-related graves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The minimal number of individuals is a calculation done to express at least the bones or the remains I have that I exhumed, excavated or I have, at least how many people do they represent. If you bear with me, I will now go on the complex side of things because it is slightly complicated but not impossible to understand, nevertheless. If we have a grave that contains 50 cadavers, the way to find out how many people are represented in that grave would be to do a head count. You just count them and you've got 50. However, if you do have a grave in which people are not complete and what you have is a combination of complete bodies and parts of bodies, legs, arms, heads, how would you choose -- or what method would you choose to count them? Let's take an example. Imagine you have a right leg and a left leg. Would you count them as one or would you count them as two? Because obviously each of the legs can belong to a different person or they can belong to the same person. So the minimal number of individuals would count them as one. So we will only use, for example, the right leg. So you have 50 right legs and you've got 50 people, irrespective of the fact that maybe the left leg or the number of left legs could be from different people but you do not count them. So it's a minimal number. But let's add another level of complexity to this. We are fine with the legs. But let's assume for a moment that all these 50 right legs are of adults, adult individuals, so which is fine. But what would happen if, in addition to that, we find some other remains, not legs, could be arms, could be skulls, that belong to children? Obviously those children would also need to be counted and added to this minimal number. And maybe these children are not represented by the right leg but are represented by some other kind of bone. For example, the sternum, a bone that lies here in the middle. That is not a paired bone, it's a unique bone. So in that case, you would count those three sternums and would add them to the 50 right legs that are adults, because the other ones are children, so your MNI, your minimal number of individuals, will be 53. So in other words, the minimal number of individuals is a way to account or to explain what this assemblage of remains or how many people are represented by that assemblage of remains. And as its name indicates, it is an underestimation, it is not an overestimation, it's an underestimation. It's a minimal number so it is likely that the real number is higher, but we would rather err on the side of underestimating than overestimating. I don't know if that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It's certainly clear enough for me and this is obviously covered in great detail in your prior testimony and in your reports, so I won't ask for any further detail. But can you say when you reached the figure of 2.541 as the smallest number of victims across these Srebrenica-related graves exhumed between 1996 and 2001. Is the process you've described basically the process that you followed in arriving at that figure?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. But there is an issue of clarification that needs to be introduced here. The report you are mentioning, with the number of 2.541 is a further calculation of the MNI. In other words, actually, the title says, "Calculating the minimum minimal number of individuals," would be the MMNI, if we have to come up with an acronym, and if I may explain the Court what it means because just not to create confusion. In that report, that is the final report, if I'm not mistaken, that I have submitted, I'm trying to merge, to come up with a single or on consolidated figure of at least how many people ICTY may have been recovering over the years. As you know, the level of complexities that people were first buried in primary sites, so in a grave, people were buried in a grave, then people were removed from that grave and their remains were scattered in a number of smaller graves. So one person could be spread out throughout many graves, the head in one place, an arm in one place, a leg in another place. Okay? Through a number of scientific analyses that I've referred to and done by other people, but they are referred to in the reports, primary graves and the so-called secondary graves were linked, for example, through soil analysis. At the moment these bodies were removed from this grave, the soil came along and was deposited in a secondary grave, so the soil here and here were the same. So a link was established. Okay? So based on that, we have to recalculate the minimal number of individuals linking this primary and secondary sites in order not to overestimate the real number of people represented by the remains that have been recovered. So, for example, if site 1 was a primary site, and site 2, 3 and 4 were the secondary sites, I would need to find a common denominator between all those sites to calculate the minimal number of individuals. That was level 1. And level 2 was that after I have calculated that merged number, I will need to calculate a minimal number of individuals based on all the remains for all the sites after being merged. So the figure of 2.541 is the most conservative, not to say extremely conservative figure of at least how many people were recovered. Because if I just added all the numbers, it would have been much more than that. And that would not be, I mean, scientifically correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just for clarification on the record, although we don't need to see it on the screen, am I correct that the report which I mentioned and where you referred to the figure of 2.541, is your January 2004 report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And that is, for the record, P938. Mr. Baraybar, at the time of your work on Srebrenica-related graves and victims, was it possible to conduct high volume DNA analysis to identify the individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not in those days. Remember that the International Commission for Missing Persons, who have been the leading DNA provider and analyser, so to call it, in the Balkans, started the operations, the massive operations, much later. I mean, I wouldn't give you an exact date but from my recollection, well into the 2000s. I mean when they started -- I mean when they got pretty much state-of-the-art technology and protocols that allowed them to work with high volume of samples. DNA analysis in that kind of scale is something very new, it's something of the last, I mean, ten years if so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the DNA identifications that have subsequently been made, using samples taken from the remains in the Srebrenica-related graves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I'm not privy to any specific information. I know it from newspapers and that, but I have not read or seen or examined any documents pertaining to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Baraybar. And I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Now we move to Mr. Tolimir and his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will be done and not necessarily mine in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were involved in the excavation of mass graves and the expert analysis of the material that was excavated, I'm sure that this was a team work which involved quite a number of different experts. Could you please tell us briefly how that team functioned? And what was the relationship between the experts on the team and what was their respective role? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. The typical exhumation team was composed by archeologists/anthropologist and I say slash because it depends on what educational system you have been trained. For example, in the United States, archaeology is a subdiscipline of anthropology; while in other countries, Europe, for instance -- in many countries in Europe, archaeology is a discipline in itself. So the field would have these archeologists/anthropologists, a photographer at least, a scene-of-crime evidence technician taking care of the evidence and logging the evidence as we would collect it, and obviously logistics support. At some point after 1997, I believe, we were able to get some facilities at the grave sites such as showers and things of the like. Therefore, there was an engineer that was assisting with the logistics. Before that, in 1996, we had a backhoe, an excavator operator, there were people supporting the team. The more -- the typical team, again, and per table, to make it simpler, would consist of a pathologist [Realtime transcript read in error "anthropologist"], an anthropologist, an autopsy technician. And people that were pretty much doing multi-tasking would be scene-of-crime officer, a photographer, sometimes the scene-of-crime officers were doing those two things. And in some occasions as well, you may have an anthropology assistant. There were people helping out cleaning or preparing some of the specimens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I hesitate to interrupt but having cleared up one mistype in the previous testimony, I see that in page 14, line 5, we have a team consisting of an anthropologist, another anthropologist. I think the word "pathologist" was used but it would probably help for the record to clear that up. I apologise, I said page 14, it's page 15, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we have two times anthropologist. But I'm not sure -- I would like to ask the witness. The sentence reads as follows: "The more -- the typical team, again, per table to make it simpler, would consist of an anthropologist, an anthropologist, and autopsy technicians. And people that were pretty much doing multi-tasking would be scene-of-crime officer," and so on. Were you referring to anthropologist and pathologists or anthropologists and archeologists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right order would be pathologist, comma, anthropologist. So pathologist first, an anthropologist, and autopsy technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That makes it clear. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, could you please tell us whether during your engagement as a member of the OTP, when you worked on the Srebrenica case, did you have a superior who gave you tasks and to whom you reported? In other words, somebody who was your boss while you were an OTP member. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There were different times in which I had different roles and I will explain that to answer your question. In 1996, as I said before, I was part of the scientific support unit. This unit was headed by Dr. Andrew Thompson, so he was my boss. In 1997, I became chief anthropologist. However, the mortuary, at any point in time, was always headed by a pathologist. Therefore, that person, and there were many of them, were my bosses. In some other occasions, as the years passed, I became chief archeologist. Therefore, I responded to the Prosecution team that would task me with the recovery of a certain site. Not that they would direct my technical work. They would just task me. And as chief anthropologist again, when I have to go back to the mortuary, I will be under the chief pathologist. That would be my boss as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So far we've had an opportunity to hear something about the relationship which exists between a pathologist and an anthropologist. Was there any co-operation between your pathologist and your anthropologist? You said that your profession is actually an anthropologist and then you joined the team as the head of that team, so can you tell us whether there was any co-operation between the two in your team and if that was indeed the case, what did that co-operation constitute of?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There was always co-operation primarily because examining remains was and is, still is, a joint effort. So when a pathologist is specialised and deals with soft tissues, obviously in ideal circumstances, a pathologist will deal with cadavers, with human cadavers, where they have organs and fluids, a pathologist will need and do need an anthropologist to work on tissues that are not his or her expertise, such as bones. Therefore, the autopsy was done as a joint effort. And primarily because we rarely encounter remains that were preserved enough as to conduct a classical autopsy, as you know, a classical autopsy would consist in opening the three cavities: The neural cavity, the chest, and the abdomen. That obviously the remains we were confronted with were extremely decomposed. They may be partly bone and part decomposing soft tissues. So there was a lot of co-operation, yes, because we have to work together. I mean, there is no way to separate things in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Baraybar, sir, in your report about the anthropological examination of mortal remains, we find not only the data that resulted from your anthropological analysis but also specific data about mass graves which are considered primary as opposed to the secondary graves. My question, based on that, would be this: Did you personally participate in the exercise to establish which mass graves were primary graves or -- and which ones were secondary graves, or did you just take over that information from the archeologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Just to be clear, are we referring to the report of December 8, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that that's mentioned in all your reports, that there is reference to primary as opposed to secondary graves. That's why I wanted to know whether you personally participated in the exercise to establish which graves were primary and which graves were secondary graves, or did you simply receive that information from your archeologists? That was my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I did participate in a number of exhumations, and through those exhumations I was able to learn what was a primary grave and what was a secondary grave. From then on, if I did receive information on the site or the exhumation of a site where I have not participated, and they refer to primary or secondary, then I knew what we were talking about. Primarily because the parameters defining a primary or a second site were well-established and I did participate in understanding what were those parameters. Do remember that I did participate in exhumations from very early on, in 1996, and that is how I got to learn these kind of things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A lot can be concluded from your answer. Mr. Baraybar, sir, in some of the graves you found bodies which were not integral, which were not complete. In some previous testimonies, we heard that each body part that was found was subject to analysis. My question is this: Based on the position of mortal remains in the graves and on some other criteria, did you try to join the different parts of the body to form one whole? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The attempt to piece body parts together would not be done at the site. And I will explain you why in a moment. However, in the mortuary, whenever possible, we looked at photographs or maps or even correlative numbers of body parts to see whether those body parts could belong to the same person. And, as a matter of fact, in some cases, we succeed at piecing together some parts, primarily on base of clothing that has been torn. Why you cannot do that during the exhumation? Because the exhumation is a process where you're recovering things in reverse. If I, to give an example, if I open a hole and put a number of people inside, and I cover it, me, as the archeologist, is doing the work in reverse. I'm first taking the fill, that is the last thing I put, and then getting to the bodies in reverse order as they were deposited. So my objective there is to record things as I see them and recover the associations that I can -- I can see, not to move one piece from one end and another one from another end and that. However, if there is something as obvious as that, that I have an arm on one side and the other arm on the other side, I will take note of it so the people in the mortuary will be able to know what I saw and put it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This means that a lot of significance was given to the notes based on the observations made at those graves, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, but I have to tell you more than no. The recording system at the exhumation site was much more comprehensive than notes. There were forms to be filled in per body or body part. There were pictures, and also there was mapping. The mapping that evolved also with time is a system by which you will take different points on the body or body part, to then represent them within the grave. So there is a wealth of documentation beyond notes. Always, the person that was in charge of the excavation would have a notebook but that is -- there is a standard archaeological procedure but irrespective of those notes, that would be like a register of the accounts of the day and specific ideas that you may have when you are excavating, there was an individual record per body or body part that would follow the remains all the way through the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. And now, please tell us, or, rather explain one of the sticking issues in this case, something that is not completely clear to any of us, I believe. As for the purpose of your analysis, how many bodies had to be completed or how complete one body had to be in order for that body to be considered complete? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The difference between a body and a body part, because that is -- I understand -- that is -- I presume what you're trying to ask me because that is in most of the reports, the term body and body part. A complete body would be a unit that would be composed of at least 75, between 70 and 75 per cent of its parts, meaning or rather namely torso, extremities, and likely head, or the complete body, minus an arm or a leg. A body part would be exactly the opposite. A body part would start from a single hand bone to, for example, a torso, a legs, one and a half legs, part of a skull. But I can concede to you right now that there isn't a scientific or metrical or quantitative way to determine what is a completes body and what is a body part. As a matter of fact, in some cases, people in the field would determine that a body part was an almost complete body and then once it got to the mortuary, the pathologist would say, You have an almost complete body for me. This is a body, not a body part. And then the record would be changed from BP, body part, to B, as in body. Having said that, the type of analysis or the detail in recording what was there or collected would not change. There is no different treatment, so to speak, to any type of remain by its completeness. We did not discriminate on how to approach remains as per they were complete or incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of this question, did you have any instances of a head being found and then marked as a body part?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm totally sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And as we know that every body has but a single head, how did you then connect that head to a body and on what basis? What was the criterion?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I explained you, we did not attempt to connect body parts unless there was sufficient evidence that one part of the body would connect with the other part of the body. And as a matter of fact, in forensic practice I would not try to fit a head on a headless body, because the only link between the two would be the joint at the first cervical vertebra, and that is not the most convincing of evidences to say this head belongs to this body, if we are talking about bones. However, what you have to bear in mind is that, yes, we did find skull pieces that were considered to be body parts, but we rarely, rarely found a complete head. Whenever we found the head, was totally fragmented, such as in the picture you saw before. In only very few cases you could find a head, a complete head. And as I said before, if there was any attempt to connect that head to a body, you would need to have a number of criteria leading you to establish an association, an extreme case would be having a body, and a complete head, a few centimetres above it or away from it that you could say that it was reasonable enough to assume that the head had been separated from the body by a number of reasons, of course, and it could be associated together. But would the mortuary have the final word in saying that actually trying every possible thing this head may belong to this body or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Can we now see in e-court Exhibit D938 or P938? This is a report by Mr. Baraybar on the minimal number of persons exhumed by the ICTY from 1996 to 2000. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I take the opportunity to put a question to the witness in the meantime? We have heard another expert witness who said, in his understanding, a body comprises more than 50 per cent of a complete body. This seems to be quite logical. Now you said today that in your way of working, you define a body at least 70 to 75 per cent of a complete body. This is, I think, a very careful estimation, but -- or calculation. You added that there is no acknowledged standard how to define a complete body or a body. What is the reason for the difference? Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the debate has been going on for many, many, years. And I believe that we have come to terms of agreeing to disagree with other colleagues. While we were working at the exhumation, you have to make sometimes certain decisions because every piece of evidence, be a body or be an artefact has been numbered or given a code. And when it came to body parts, you have to define what would be a B or a BP; a body or a body part. And there were a number of considerations there, and I think that one of the main considerations would be the likelihood that that unit would be able to yield some information, some useful information, and eventually of course be identified. And it was very difficult to define how far would you go with a body part or how far would you go with a body. Because you could have a hand or you could have a hand with the arm and half of the torso or maybe the torso with an arm. And how would you call that a body or a body part? In my case, I settled very much for a body to be a much more complete unit, a much, much more complete unit. So it was a body minus certain parts. But anything below that would be a body part. And the other issue that comes out of this is, in not being a sort of a scientific way to define it, is that this situation was so new. Prior to 1996, I would dare to say no one had been encountering the sheer volume of fragmented people or people, I mean, shredded to pieces. And the first logic is to call it body part. But, I mean, the first day we coined that term, I don't think we actually knew what were the boundaries of that because every site would pose further levels of complexity. Just to share with you what this means is that imagine that there were some sites that the preservation of the remains were such that the flesh and the fat has turned into what we call adipocere. It's like a body wax, so to speak. So you had limbs, and obviously you could distinguish limbs as body parts if you have an arm or a leg, but there were other sites where the remains were totally skeletonised. There were only bones, not even articulated. So they all were body parts and could range from, as I said, one hand bone to half a skeleton. So I would say that, yes, I stick in a way with my definition, understanding that we will have some disagreements, so to speak. But for me, in any way, a much more semantic disagreements because the analysis is not dependent in a way on the integrity of the remains. As a matter of fact, because the integrity of the remains, and this variability on the integrity of the remains is that we have calculated, for example, the minimal number of individuals rather than counting arms or legs and units of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want some information, if you have, in relation to the team with which you worked. Was there someone in your team who would be responsible for securing the scenes of crimes, say the graves? By securing, I mean preserving them as items of evidence. Did you have such a person in your team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1996, we had a security presence on the grounds to obviously keep the site intact, from anybody coming after we have left. In 1996, I recall that the problem there was is that NATO, at the time IFOR, if I'm not mistaken, was reluctant to guard the graves. They would say they were there to be protection to the people, meaning the team, us, but not to guard any grave. So in those days, we used to sleep next to the graves, to force the soldiers to guard us and the graves. Luckily for us, in the years that came later, ICTY provided a permanent security detachment from The Hague or another office to actually guard the site after hours. And as I said, these also saw some improvement in the conditions of work, having, for example, showers, they were something quite necessary, and then these guards could actually physically stay there and protect the integrity of the evidence that we left behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: After you left, was there an attempt then to also secure the sites in the sense that the future generations of people wanted to visit the site, they would clearly see where the grave was and the location? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We did not. All the sites were actually excavated and then back-filled, primarily because the areas where we excavated we did not know were public property or public property, and we did not know either nor we wanted to cause any problems for the population living in the area by, for example, leaving an open hole and these holes were sometimes quite deep and could get filled with water so it could be dangerous for a child to drown or something of the kind. So we did not leave anything -- anything open. But I would like to just to let you know something I remember now, that pertains somewhat to your first question, and is that during 1996, and 1997, although in 1997 we did not dealt with a case pertaining to this trial, there were a number of security issues and we had to evacuate the sites in many occasions because of -- there were riots by the civilian population and we have to literally run out of the site and this happened at least one occasion in 1996, or at least one occasion I can remember, if not two, my memory, I mean, falls me a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Baraybar, I have a question, a qualification regarding terminology. In the transcript, on page 194, I'm looking at the line 4 on page 194, so lines 4 to 6, you are talking about the skeletised body parts or the skeletised body, the overall remains of the skeletal body, which are nothing but bones, non-articulated bones. And which make the body. The question that I have for you is this: I would like to know when would that be an entire body, without soft tissues and without fluids? So when would that be an entire body? Would that be actually an entire body or just a body parts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I reply in French? It would be easier for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course you can, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When I spoke about body parts, irrespective of the fact whether it was a skeleton or whether it still retained some soft tissue, when we referred to body parts, we do so, we refer to body parts because these are somebody's remains. Those remains may be bones, they may be larger parts, larger parts of the body, like legs or arms. It can be the skeleton, or it also can be tissue. The actual stage in which a part of the body is, is of no bearing at all on the actual state of preservation of a single part, if I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, you have been quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put the same question very simple way for a better understanding of myself? Skeleton without any soft tissues, is that a body or a body part? I mean a complete skeleton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A complete skeleton is a body. It's definitely a body. And, Your Honour, just to, I mean, be more purist, if I may, obviously in a complete skeleton, considering there is no soft tissues, it is likely that little parts like the finger bones will be lost, but will still be a body. It will be an exaggeration to expect to find a skeleton with every single bone and nails, that would be an almost impossibility in those conditions, in a grave with dozens of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. Thank you, Judges. I thank all the members of the Trial Chamber for helping us clarify this issue. Can we now see, please, page 5 in the Serbian language and page 4 in the English language of the document which I requested previously? In the English, this is the last part, the last portion above the numbers 1, 2 and 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, we now have it. I'm quoting a part of this report: "The purpose of this report is, however, to provide the minimum number of persons exhumed from the Srebrenica graves between 1996 and 2001. In order to calculate such a figure, a number of assumptions were proceeded from. First, whenever multiple grave sites were thought to contain victims from the same event, they were merged together and then merged again with the remains found in secondary sites. "2. All primary and secondary sites were merged. "3. In order to merge the remains from all the grave sites, the same bones had to be used in all counts. "The minimal number of persons, of individuals, was established on the basis of the age structure and therefore not always the same bones were used to calculate the distinct intervals."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the English page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Fifth, the most frequent types of bones were obtained from primary grave sites and were used for the secondary ones." Did I understand correctly that in item 1, you're actually referring to two assumptions, the first one that the victims actually were the victims of the same event and the second is a -- assumption is that of their merging with the remains found in secondary grave sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The way I see it is that we referring to event as the relationship between sites, in this case primary and secondary sites, that have been linked by a number of scientific tests that has been also referred to in my reports and have been done by other people. I do not know if I'm answering your question, because that is what I understood from your question but you may please -- I mean, ask me again to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall clarify it by this question. Seeing as you are an anthropologist and not a military expert or an OTP investigator, can you tell us who gave you the information on the basis of which you assumed that the victims from the different graves were -- actually came to grief in the same event, were the victims of the same event as is stated under item 1 here?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I said, I do not mean event but by any other type of event that for me is the relationship between a primary and a secondary site. So I will provide you with some examples of how I got to the conclusion, as a matter of fact not me, but based on those reports, that sites were linked. Among the evidence that I quote are the reports of Dr. Brown, who did the analysis of soil, as I explained before, comparing the soil found in primary sites and in secondary sites. Discovering the soil was the same, and this was established as a link. But let me be more specific because that may lead to confusion. And I'll try to be very, very simple in this explanation because it is quite complicated, I understand that, and I hope you can bear with me. I want to take a totally hypothetical example to make it easier. Imagine you have a grave that is dug in sand or a sandy soil. You put a number of people inside and you cover it. Sometime afterwards, I go in and excavate these bodies, trying to empty this grave, to, I presume, destroy the evidence or hide it or something. And I will remove the bodies with an excavator, and put them in a truck, take it away and go to another location where the soil is a clay soil, totally different, not sand but clay. I will open a hole in the clay, and then I'm going to take my bodies in the truck and put them back into that hole. Obviously, since I have used excavators to remove the bodies, I'm not only removing bodies, I'm also removing the soil that is with the bodies. So that sand now has been redeposited into a hole that was dug in clay. So when I dig that secondary site and I find that sand, I will say, Well, this sand does not belong here because it's clay. So Dr. Brown examined those kind of links, and through those links he was able to establish that there were sites that were linked and if they were linked, that is what I refer to as an event. In other words, if I find an individual in grave A that is a primary grave, and other pieces in grave B, that is secondary grave I would say they are linked and they are part of the same event. It doesn't mean, and I'm not implying that this happened at the same time, that is that the same day they bury them, the same day they open a secondary grave, That is not what I'm talking about. Event I mean as this link.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Please be so kind as to explain this also. In item 1, you also refer to the collecting of the remains in a single spot and I presume that is done by experts. Tell me, was this the physical relocation of bones to a single spot and if that had been the case, who did that and under whose supervision were the bones thus collected in a single place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You refer, sorry, you refer item 1 on page 4 of the report, in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There may be a translation issue. When I mean merging, I mean calculations. I'm not talking about physically putting bodies together between primary and secondary sites. This is referring to merging numbers. I may -- if you wish, I may expand on this to make it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be grateful if you could expand and make things a bit clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We are talking here about how to come up with a number, right? A minimal number of individuals. So let me explain exactly what I mean. And we are going to take another hypothetical example, that is pretty much what I'm saying here. This is not hypothetical but I would like to take a hypothetical example just to illustrate this. We have a primary grave, for this matter a grave, that contains a number of people, let's say 100 people for simplicity. At some point in time, I go in and I scoop out some of the contents of this grave, or most of the contents or all the contents of the grave. But let's assume that I scoop out 80 people, okay? And I leave 20 people behind. But these 20 people behind that I'm leaving behind in the grave may be totally cut up in pieces because, as I said I'm using a machine, I'm not going in with a trowel and a brush. I'm actually excavating so that what I may leave behind is a number of body parts or incomplete remains that represent 20 people. Then I do open five other holes and those 80 people will be now spread or scattered through these five holes, some pieces here, some pieces there, some pieces there. The question is: How would I be able to calculate the minimal number of people represented by hole 1, the primary site, and the five other holes? First, I need to know that the sites are related. How do I know that? Through, for example, soil analysis, as Dr. Brown did. So site 1 was excavated in sand and then I found the same sand in a clay matrix in five different holes. So condition 1 is fulfilled. The sites are related. What I now need to do is to try to merge, in terms of numbers, some to come up with figure that represents all these six locations, number 1 and five others. So if I , for example, was to do a minimal number of individuals per grave, say, in the grave 1 I may have 20, okay? But, for example, in grave 1, the secondary -- grave 2, sorry, the secondary grave, I may encounter that the most common bone or body part is the right leg, while in the other one was the left arm. And then I move to another secondary site and I will find that the right foot is more common, and so on and so forth. So if I was to just add the numbers that I would get in each of the graves, my total would likely be higher to the original number of people that were in that grave, that was a hundred, as I said. I may come up with 130 because if I just add different frequencies of different things, I'm not counting the same thing. So by merging, I mean that I have to find a common denominator among all the graves, the primary grave and the secondary grave, so if it is a right leg so the right leg will be. And based on that, I will calculate the minimal number of individuals. Therefore, my final number will be a very conservative number that is an underestimate of the real number of people that were found in the grave. Otherwise, I will be very liberal, and being very liberal I will be increasing or swelling up the real number of victims that were there. I do not know whether that was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. We must have the first break now, Mr. Tolimir, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May I ask, Mr. Baraybar, to explain to us paragraph number 5? Actually, item number 5 in the paragraph which I quoted. You say the most frequent type of bone was the derived from the primary sites and then applied to the secondary sites. Please be so kind as to clarify this to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Of course. As I explained before, we were able to define what was a primary site and what was a secondary site. Following this line of thought, if a primary site is a place where bodies were disposed in the first place, and from there removed, to be placed in secondary sites, any calculation should originate at the primary site. And while this is a totally arbitrary decision, it is the most logical decision, not to overestimate the number of bodies you may be counting. So you would say that whatever was the most type, common type of bone in the primary site, the place where everything originated from, you would use the same type of bone to calculate your MNI in retrospect, so on the secondary sites. So if in site 1 you had the left leg bone as the most common bone, that would be the bone you will be using throughout the secondary sites. With the exception, of course, as I mentioned at the beginning, that you had, for example, individuals of another age that were not represented by these left legs. So, for example, you may have a right arm of somebody that was on a totally different age than the previous example I gave you. So if all these left legs were of adults and you happened to have a right arm of a child, that would count as one. But you will use the same type of bone starting from the primary to the secondary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. And now could we look at page 4 in the Serbian language, paragraph 1, and page 4 in the English language, also paragraph 1. We are talking about the MNI and when you talk about the MNI, you defined this as the minimum number of individuals necessary to explain all of the elements of the collection of the remains. And you point to the origin, White, 1991, page 278, and did you find this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you please check the number of the page in English again? Is that the right one we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first paragraph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes. In other words, the minimum number of individuals is the number that you need to account for all the pieces that you have found, but it is, yet again, as its name implicates, a minimal number, not a maximal number, so something would be totally different would be that you were estimating the maximum number of individuals in which you would need to account for every possible piece as potentially representing somebody else. But, yes, it means that if I have an assemblage of bones, of remains, the minimal number would account or would tell me at least how many people those bones represent. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain, or could you please tell us, who Mr. White is and which of his publications are you referring to in here? I don't see his publication in the bibliography of the works that you used while compiling your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You're totally right. His name is not listed here. But it may, hopefully, be listed elsewhere and let me find out for you. If I'm not mistaken, it's a book called "Human Osteology." Mr. White is a quite well known physical anthropologist who works in a number of archaeological and paleoanthropological sites throughout the world who has extensive experience working with fragmentary remains, hence he's quoted in this -- in this report. But you are totally right, I have omitted the quotation, as I have seen also many typos and things of the kind, regrettably, but thank you for pointing that out to me. I'm trying to see whether I have quoted it anywhere else. And it seems I haven't, as a matter of fact. It is -- I have overlooked to include that quote. Let's see. I'm not losing the hope that it may be at least in another report. Nope. It seems I have not quoted Mr. White, but the book will be called "Human Osteology."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. And now could you tell us whether all mortal remains had to find their place when you determined the minimum number of individuals, or, rather, did you take into account only particular parts of each of the skeletons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I did not understand the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat. Thank you. Did every mortal remain have to find its own place when you set out to determine the minimum number? Or did you take into account only particular parts of the skeleton? If we look at your previous answer, you said that a minimum number is necessary to define the assemblage of your remains. And my question is whether every part of the assemblage had have to find its own place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. We prepared inventories of every single bone in the skeleton. The minimum number of individuals was calculated by seeing what was the most frequent bone or part of bone in all those inventories. Just to give you an idea of how exhaustive this process was made, whenever you had a long bone, for example the leg bone, we did record whether the bone was complete, meaning whether the top part that was called the proximal part, the middle part and the distal or the end of the bone was complete and we would say, 1, 1, and 1, that would be the value of 1, means presents and 0 would be absent. Because in some occasions, the minimal number was calculated based on, for example, the upper part of the leg bone from the right side, so all I'm trying to say is that we did not only do a count, like how many legs or how many this, but we subdivided bones inasmuch as possible in the most discrete units, to make the calculations. So if I'm understanding your question correctly, the answer is yes, we have exhausted recording every possible recordable thing, and based on that, calculate the minimal number, so it's not been a kind of leg count or hand count or something. It's using very discrete categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Please, what I see here is that when you determined the minimum number of individuals, you used several reports. My question is this: Do you know if anybody else but you carried out any analysis in order to establish the minimum number of persons in order to perhaps double check your results or for some other reason? I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not know whether anybody else has attempted to recalculate what I have done. That I do not know. In my case, what I can say is that these calculations are totally arithmetic. They are not complex calculations of any kind. There is no statistics. There is no projections. It's just pretty much sums and subtractions of numbers. This information that has been done obviously on a number of reports, and has not been very easy, has been done once and again and again and again and again, because in adding all these numbers sometimes you would -- I mean, get it wrong for -- you do a wrong calculation and you get two more or one less, and numbers didn't then fit. But as per your question, if somebody else has done this? Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, during the period that your report refers to, are you saying that this should be the MNI 2.541 as you stated during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. The final minimal -- minimal number of individuals, meaning after we have merged every possible piece of information we had until that date, meaning January 2004, the number will remain at 2.541.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Mr. Baraybar, before 2004, before you submitted this report, did you hear any criticism of the methodology that you used in order to establish your MNI or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. I've heard many criticisms regarding many things but not that specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in professional criticism, criticism coming from your fellow professionals who deal with the MNI establishment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 6 of the report in Serbian and in English? We are interested in establishing the age of the bodies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the page in front of you. And you say, and I quote. This is from your report: "Age was estimated, in other words age was estimated." My question is this: The results that you obtained while establishing the age, were they just estimates? And if so, how reliable those estimates are?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: When you deal with remains of any kind, what you perform is an estimation. Age has -- there is two types of aging, if we can call it that way. One is chronological aging, that is the one that would be on your ID card, the day you were born and you can calculate how many years and months and days and even hours and whatever unit you want to use to estimate your chronological age. However, when you do have a body, you estimating biological age. Biological age is how your body looks like. That's a very simple way to put it. So let me give you an example. If you -- if we were looking at, for example, the knee joint to estimate age, that is not the case, and you happen to be a soccer player, at the year 35, your knee will look like you were 80 because the wear and tear of your activity. That is why we use certain elements that are known to change with age. For example, as in this case, the fourth rib or the pubic symphysis. All estimates are subject to variation and that is why you cannot provide a specific pin-point age. You cannot say this person is 44.5 years or 44 years, six months, and three days. Obviously you cannot. Therefore, the estimate is an estimate that is given within a bracket, because you know that that bracket would provide you what is called accuracy. It would not provide you precision. It would provide you accuracy. So to give you an example, it would be accurate to say that all individuals within this courtroom are between - I'll be generous - 10 and 100 years. We are totally accurate. But we are very imprecise. Precision will be to give the specific age estimate of each of the persons in this courtroom. Likewise, dealing with remains, our estimates have to be based on very robust techniques, and robust I mean that I cannot use a standard for aging remains that has been based on two cases or five or ten. I have to use samples that statistically make a difference. And this means that the bracket estimate I get is a bracket estimate with some confidence, speaking statistics, would be a confidence interval, meaning that most of the times I'll be right and only sometimes I'll be wrong. That's what statistics mean at the end of the day. So, yes, it is an estimate, but the validity of the estimate is based on the type of techniques that we have used to estimate age. So age has not been estimated by, let's say, eyeballing, by picking up a bone and saying well, to me, it's like 35. And that is not science. And that is why you would appreciate that how conservative we have been with age estimation, perhaps too conservative, meaning that there is a large number of people that fall on the interval 25 and plus. That in terms of forensic cases, if you had one case, let's assume that you working in the mortuary and you have only one case, it will be totally absurd to say this person is anywhere between 25 and plus, could be 25 and a hundred. Could be half of the population. However, why did we do that? Because it's a robust standards for aging could only be observed in certain parts of the body, not in all parts of the body. So if I found a hand or a foot or a piece of a leg, maybe then I would only be able to say this is an adult, there is no features of being somebody younger, it's an adult, but how old is this person, I do not know. And this was different if I found a piece of the body where I could observe the techniques I have listed here that we have used, in which case you could be more precise. In the rest of the cases you only would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. In the first passage you describe the methods that you used for identification or, rather, for establishing the age of the bodies, and you are probably referring to scientific publications and their authors. My question is this: Are these methods generally accepted at the time when you carried out your research, were there any other methods used in order to establish the age of the mortal remains? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, there are plenty more of techniques that can be used to age human remains. And that is not the issue. The issue is whether those techniques have been developed in populations that could be called forensic populations, that bear some kind of resemblance, at the very least, with the population we are dealing with. In other words, what would be the use for me to, for example, apply some of the techniques that were available at the time and still are by Professor Lovejoy and colleagues from Case Western Reserve University? While these techniques are very comprehensive, the population from which they were derived is a prehistoric, native, North American population from Ohio. So it is obvious that I would not be able to apply a technique derived from a prehistoric North American population to a contemporary European population. That would be unscientific. On the other hand, all the techniques that were used here have been derived from either forensic populations, for example Suchey -- the Suchey-Brooks technique is a technique that was derived from a sample from the office of the coroner in Los Angeles county, very large hundreds of individuals dying in Los Angeles. It's a contemporary population. Likewise, the Ishian [phoen] loss technique; while Smith, for example, for the dental classification of the teeth is derived from a number of samples that were pulled together but all of them are from recent -- I mean, living, as a matter of fact, children. So all I'm trying to say is that not because there are techniques available, you can use them all. Because not all of them may be applicable. Because many of them could have been derived in populations that do not fit into the criteria that we looking for, meaning a recent population. It is extremely unwise to simply extrapolate results from one setting and blindly applying to another. Because then what we going to get are results that are totally meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. To explain this in full, you say what is referred to by Simmons et al in 1999 were modified. Actually this Suchey-Brooks and symphyseal phases were modified using the population-specific standards for Bosnians described by Simmons et al. My question is: What are symphyseal phases, that's one; and secondly, what are population-specific standards for Bosnians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: How to explain you. A little bit of mimic because I don't have any other means to show you. The pubic symphysis is, if I can stand up for a second, is this part here. So you got your pelvis that has two sides, right, and they meet right here. So if you actually touch here, you're going to feel something that is like a boney part. So the pubic symphysis are the two faces that meet like this and you're looking at this face. There is a -- not a cartilage but a fibrous component between the two, okay, and you're looking at this face. This face that is like this, changes with age in males and females. So the older you get there is a number of changes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin. Sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting as well, both you, Mr. Baraybar and to General Tolimir. If it would help, and I don't know if General Tolimir wants to use it, but Prosecution Exhibit P1050 shows a graphical picture of a pelvis and if the description is going to get any more complicated than we just saw, it would certainly help me and perhaps others to have that image available for the description.

So what you see in the drawing is this: Imagine that you open it like this, so the pubic symphysis is that phase there that is covered on the illustration. Does it help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It helps and just for the record, first, the witness drew a circle, explaining the subpelvic angle; is that correct?

utterances.text: Angle, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. We are grateful. I should only like the witness to say for the transcript whether these Simmons standards are generally accepted standards for the establishment of age at the moment of death on the basis of mortal remains. Thank you.

utterances.text: Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should just like to apologise. It is Simmons in the transcript. We should like to ask the witness to spell the name of this standard exactly so that it could be faithfully recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Simmons. It's S-i-m-m-o-n-s, Simmons.
