utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the exhibit number D131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the time when all these studies were made, it was a valid correction of the Suchey-Brooks technique. Remember this standard was a correction only for the pubic symphysis, so it's not an all-out aging standard. It's something that refers to a specific technique on a specific bone. And obviously this standard now has been improved on further in 2008 that was not relevant for the time the report was produced but obviously and luckily science progresses and improvements can be made over the years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now a question from Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to ask more specifically since you mentioned the fact that you also worked in ICTR, Rwanda, would the population-specific standard go down to ethnic identification, for example? In the case of Rwanda, would you be able to identify the bones being Tutsi or Hutu or Twa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is nothing to do with ethnicity as such but something we call biological affinity, that has nothing to do with ethnicity. But it is a fact that, for example, the rate of maturation, let's assume, for example, females, the rate of maturation of females is different between, for example, Africans, North Americans, Europeans and even Latin Americans. If you, for example, live in a high altitude place like in my country, if you live at 4.000 metres above sea level, you will develop fully but you will be shorter, because your system, that is extremely intelligent, is deciding that what you need is to complete yourself as a functional human being in detriment of stature, for example. So these details are very important because I cannot go to the Congo and apply Peruvian standards because maybe I'll be underaging or overaging people in the Congo, and if I take Congolese standards to Peru, it would be the same thing. My people will look much younger than what they are and maybe they are older because, for example, they are smaller. So it has nothing to do with ethnicity, in that regard. And, of course, the specific issue of Rwanda would deserve another session to discuss but I fully appreciate the very intelligent question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Judge Nyambe. Thank you, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you have just said in response to Judge Nyambe's question, please tell us whether on your team there had been persons who had earlier dealt with the establishment of the age of persons at the time of death, persons who originated in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: None of the people that worked in the teams had been doing any research, if that is what you're asking, regarding the Bosnian population or population of the Balkans, I mean not in those days, not that I can recall. I'm sure -- I mean nobody had. Maybe later but not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was rather interested, in fact, whether on your team there had been persons with experience in estimating the age of persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina in this particular context, in view of what you've just said in relation to Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. But okay, I may need to clarify this. The issue is not whether you are experienced in working with a specific population, because the standards are the same. In other words, all us human beings share the same characteristics. In other words, there is no -- I mean, phenotypical differences in the pubic symphysis, whether I'm looking at an African person or a Latin American person or a Bosniak or Russian, or whatever, it doesn't really matter. Our bone structure are pretty much the same in that respect. It's not whether I'm an expert in looking at Bosnian pubic symphysis because the pubic symphysis is the same no matter where I am. What changes is the age brackets associated to each of these categories. So, for example, if we were to divide, as it is divided, this technique into six phases, phase 1 for a Peruvian population could be an interval between, let's say, 16 and 23 or something of the kind. Maybe for the Balkans it will be 18 to 25. And maybe in Africa would be 16 to 19. And maybe elsewhere something else. But the features are the same. So it doesn't really matter whether you have experience in that population. There is no special quality you could observe in a given population that will tell you, yes, I mean, this definitely will be different. I mean, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have partially responded to what I also meant to ask you now, but let us now look at page 10 in Serbian and page 8 in English of this report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Exhibit P938. Thank you, Aleksandar. Thank you. Here we have a table or, rather, we do not have it right now in front of us, but it will reappear on the screen so that we can see it. Page 10 in Serbian and page 8 in English, please. Thank you. Could we also have page 10 in Serbian? Well, the figures are the same anyway. We see a table here. The age brackets are indicated at the top, from 8 to 12, from 13 to 17, from 15 to 24, 25 plus, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why is this specific age -- why was this specific age bracket taken, 15 to 24? How is it scientifically justified? How is it scientifically relevant, that specific age bracket, in order to establish the time of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The -- as I explained at the beginning, we are estimating biological age, and that means that we would create a bracket, an interval, within which the age of the person should be. That is the way to be accurate. These four stages correspond to developmental stages that are observable. I will give you an example. How did we come up with the age of 8 to 12? Okay. Eight to 12 means that the person cannot be or should not be, that is better to say, should not be older than 12, nor younger than 8, okay? How is it characterised? Well, is it characterised by some features of the teeth? And how certain teeth have grown? And that is based, for example, on the standard by Smith that I have quoted here from 1991 or 1981. Well, you know that an individual that had, for example, the first molar, one of the back teeth, that has grown up to a certain extent, you know that that happens within this and that year. Not before not after. That's one thing. If you combine this with, for example, the pelvic bone, the same -- I mean the pelvic bone that we saw before, the pelvic bone between 8 and 12 is actually separated into three parts. And only later on is that fusing to become one part. Okay? So if you find these elements together with size, for example, you would say comfortably that this person is within that age bracket. But beware. This does not mean that an individual that was between 8 and 12 could not in absolute terms be in the next interval of 13 to 17, okay? But what do I mean by this? If I decided to put it in the interval 8 to 12, it's because there is enough elements that made this person a young person, and if I decided to put somebody in the next category, it's because there is enough elements that make this person older than the previous one. Now, I'm totally conscious that it is meant to be an overlap because we are talking about brackets, intervals, not chronological age. So somebody between 8 to 12 could be 12.9, but I have no way to know it. All I know is that based on all these elements, and I'm observing, it is most likely that this person falls in this category rather than the other one. And that is why you see this division. So it is not a division that a -- a capricious division that I decided to invent to see what do I do with all these people? I put some here and put some there. All of them are supported by specific morphological elements that reflect what I explained the Judge a moment ago and that is this developmental patterns. Likewise, somebody who is 25 plus is somebody who has everything fused. You know that children are very plastic, you know. They are very plastic. It's very easy to dress them, I mean. As a matter of fact, you see the clothing of a baby is very small and then you say, How I am going to fit this baby? And the baby is very plastic. Why is that? Because the bones are composed primarily by cartilage, and when this bone unit replaces the cartilage, the individual grows by the ends, by the extremities. So it means that the extremities of the bones until puberty, more or less, are open, are separated. And when you become an adult they become fused. So by the same token, if I find a leg that is totally fused, I know that this person must be at least 25 years of age. But I do not know if the person is 23.5. Because there is bound to be variability. That's a fact. I don't know whether I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain to me what is the scientific explanation or justification for this range, 15 to 24, because it seems quite big, and while we are on this subject -- on the subject, there are two age brackets shown in the table, 13 to 17 and 15 to 24, and they overlap in 13 to 17 and 15 to 24 overlap. Can you explain that too to me so those would be two questions.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The variation of the age ranges had to do primarily, if we compare this from 1996 and after, by the increase in the number of body parts that we were finding and the inability in some cases to be more precise in our age estimate. So, for example, some of the elements I've been telling you compromise a number of bones, teeth and long bones, for example, but in some cases you would find only one or the other. So it will be very difficult to combine these elements. That is one factor. The second factor is that these age ranges are also made in order to consolidate some of the data that was collected in 1996, and the data collected in 1996 did not follow a specific order of organisation. Many of them were spreadsheets with the individual ages given by anthropologists per case, so what we need to do is to take these hundreds of cases and present them in some kind of fashion, because otherwise what I would have provided you with is hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of reports for you to figure out how many people you had and what age distribution. So this overlap that you see there reflects also that. They are not as big as you think. But they reflect two types of situations. The 13 to 17 is an individual characterised as a young juvenile, somebody in the early puberty, while the second category is somebody evolving to the late part of the puberty. So if we are to imagine for a moment what would you expect to find in the bone, in the first category of 13 to 17 will be an individual which long bones are still growing, that the epiphysis, I mean the parts, the extremities that articulate of the bone would be separated, totally separated, while when looking at the second category, you'll be looking at a bone that has almost completed growth, with partial fusion of these extremities. That would be - obviously I'm oversimplifying things - some of the features. But there is bound to be some overlap, and where are we getting the information for the cutting point? The information for the cutting point is obtained from standards of the fusion of a number of bones, from a very large, and I would say the only one available, forensic sample that used American soldiers that died in Korea, and some in Vietnam as well but primarily Korea. This is a sample that include a variety of biological affinities, people classified as Hispanics and people from Oriental ancestry, African Americans, a number of people. But this is the only comprehensive sample that exists to date pretty much. That is Stewart -- McKern and Stewart, and that is listed in the bibliography.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Could you please tell us whether there were any cases where you found only parts of bodies in a grave, and did you have a problem then to establish the age, if you only found parts of a body? How did you manage to establish their year of birth, their age in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I said before, age, estimation is limited by how complete the remains may be. I mean, some cases, not some, but many cases all you were able to say is that this person is an adult; young adult, middle adult, senile, impossible to say. You had a bone, for example, that was all fused and you couldn't say anything else. So it did happen. But I mean that is why these categories from 25 onwards are so broad. 25 plus could occupy half of a population. We couldn't say more. However, it's easier to age younger people, because younger people have much more elements of unfused parts, of growing parts, that are much more visible. But all the people, meaning a generic adult, is virtually impossible if you have, of course, this -- a body part or a bone, a rib, a clavicle, if everything is fused all you can say is it's an adult. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page 9 in e-court. Page 9 in Serbian and page 7 in English. The title is, "The age of bodies" and I'm going to quote a part of that text. Thank you. We don't have it yet. No, no, we do, we do. I can see it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Age," it says here: "This review combines data collected over a number of years using different aging standards. During the 1996 to 1999 campaigns or, rather to 2001, most aging indicators were derived from modern North American populations. Only after 1999 population-specific standards were used." My question is this: The data obtained before 1999, could they be updated based on some previous reports, photos, or a review of the bones in order to apply a unique criterion to establish the age of the remains? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it would. But let me -- so everybody is clear regarding this. When I say the different aging standards means only one thing. In 1996, they applied in addition to the standards we have been using throughout, some other observations. But the common element throughout the years is the fourth rib, the pubic symphysis and all that as explained in these reports. In 1996 it added some other observations. Some people were looking at, for example, if I'm not mistaken, I mean, it's my pure recollection here, they were looking at the fusion of the -- of some part of the vertebra for subadults, okay, for example. But we found, or I found, that that study had a very small sample, population sample, to begin with, so it wasn't very robust and also it depended to find a spine and that wasn't always the case, and some specific vertebra in the spine, not the whole spine but just some specific vertebra. As for your question whether we could now revisit everything, yes, it is possible. The question is: What would we obtain? The variation that exist between the estimates of Suchey-Brooks that is based on North American multi-racial, as they call it, population from Los Angeles and the Bosnian standards is that according to the study of Simmons, people look slightly older per phase. So if phase 1 as I said in North American population is - I'm just making this up - 15 to 20, in Bosnia would be 17 to 23, for example. Okay? The range. But if we do that, then we would need to use an even more robust population-specific sample that was published only in 2008 and is based on 891 cases that combines Kosovo, some of Bosnia and some of Croatia, so it's a very robust thing, but again the differences per phase would be extreme. It's not that phase 1 suddenly becomes a year 50 years old, I mean that is not the case. There are differences, but I mean they are settle differences. Then would it be reflected in these estimates? No, it would not. Because the people that are 25 plus will remain 25 plus. You will be more precise, not more accurate. So as per the young people, this will -- these will remain where they are because that technique I'm telling you about is a technique dealing with the Suchey-Brooks technique for the pubic symphysis, not with anything else. So, yes, you could do it, but you'll get pretty much back to the same results because these categories have been kept as wide as possible exactly to avoid that type of problem. Because it will be too pretentious to be precise when you have only bits and pieces to work with. You're not talking about complete cadavers but primarily body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page 7 in Serbian and page 6 in English? We are interested in the part which speaks about gender and how to establish the gender of any mortal remains. Could this be blown up for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the last sentence here, where it says sex, in the last sentence of this paragraph, you say: "When dealing with body parts or isolated bones, only the morphology of the pelvic girdle was used in determining sex." My question is this: Was it just this method and its application that led to the determination of the gender of a number of persons, while the gender of some other persons remained undetermined? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. As you know, the safest way to sex a body will be with external genitalia. Because the expression of sex in the skeleton, at least, could vary from people that are -- that -- for example, for males, from people very masculine features, I mean boney structure, to people that may be very gracile. So if you are looking at the bones of people, you could be confused in some cases. Therefore, when you only have bones, you have to start with the pelvis. And why is that? There is a reason for that. The reason being that there is a structural and functional difference between the female and male pelvis. The female pelvis is prepared for child bearing or child birth, while not the male one. And this will cause structural differences that would make possible to differentiate male from females. If I do not have the pelvis, I would use the skull, but the skull already is much less efficient to discriminate between males and females because there are no structural differences or functional differences between the female and male skull. If I don't have a skull, I would use the long bones, but long bones means that I assume that men are taller and more robust than women and women are shorter and more gracile. But that is totally absurd because in a specific population, it could be the reverse or it could be that women are carrying out tasks that men carry in other populations. So how would I be conservative? By simply sexing feet and hands and whatever, or just concentrating myself on the most robust indicator and that is why we have a tremendous number of undetermined individuals, meaning obviously the sex of that body part is something that can be known but we cannot grasp it, we cannot extract it from those remains because they are very incomplete. So yet again, we are erring on the side of conservatism in terms of estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. The fact is that in a population of the same ethnic origin, there are people who are all smaller built or bigger built. Some people who are shorter and taller, of different body shapes in other words. Do these differences have an impact on determining how old was the person at the moment of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It does, but it depends as well what type of feature I'm looking at. As I gave you the example at the beginning, if I'm examining people that were playing soccer, these people at 35 will have the knees of somebody of 70 or 80, so if my indicator for age will be the wear and tear of the knee, what I would be concluding would be totally spurious. But, for example, the pubic symphysis is an area that is not subject to specific stress, so to speak. Obviously there is differences in women regarding child birth and all the rest of it, but I mean -- or the fourth rib is not an area that I'm actually using, it's an area protected by cartilage and I'm only breathing pretty much. But other parts of the body that if I was looking at them and trying based on that to estimate age, it will be totally wrong. And believe it or not, it would have been very tempting to use some age indicators that have been derived from prehistoric or medieval populations in Europe where they used, for example, the amount of leaping of the vertebra of the back. You may have heard about this parrot beak, meaning that the vertebral bodies have this overgrown and sometimes you got back pain because it's piercing a nerve. But, of course, if you look at somebody who is been carrying weights all his life, let's take as an example somebody from my country, somebody working in a farm that is carrying tremendous weights since age 8 or 10, this person at 20 will look skeletally much older if I'm looking at the spine, for example. But if I'm looking at other areas that are more discrete and that are changing with age irrespective of work, it will be totally different. Hence, the choice of the standards we have chosen. Yet again, more conservatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Do you know why, from 2001 onwards, exhumations were given to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Does it have the same type of expert bodies as your team, the team that was involved in exhumations from 1996 to 2001? And during that period, performed only 2.541 exhumations which shows how meticulous you were in your work? In other words, will this development have an impact on the quality of the work performed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Just a correction on the transcript here. We did not perform 2.541 exhumations. We calculated a minimal minimum number, so MMNI, of individuals, of 2.541, just for the record. Because in line 10, I believe, it says that we performed 2.541 exhumations. I do not know, I think -- I mean I'm the wrong person to ask why the Tribunal gave -- if it gave anything to the government of Bosnia to perform these things and I'm not acquainted at all with the quality of work they do or anything of the kind. I have not been involved with their work nor been following their work. Very shortly after I was in Kosovo, so I have no more knowledge than you. All I know is from the media and things of that kind but I have no comment to make regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know anything that would explain why the establishment of the MNI, as you corrected me, was taken out of the hands of the OTP and given into the hands of the bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I don't know. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the provider of the funds have anything to do with that? And the funds referred to in here are those applied to the DNA analysis and other such methods used in your work.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I mean, the providers of what funds have anything to do with what? I don't understand. You may rephrase or repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that restricted by the funds which are allocated to establish the final number? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I ignore if funds have anything to do with these calculations. I mean, as I have said before, I was employed by the Tribunal and my duty was to prepare these expert reports, and I ignore I mean whether there were funds or not. I mean, those kind of questions I think pertain more to the OTP than to me, in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to hear that from you as an expert who was engaged for a number of years. I wanted to hear your opinion. I would like to thank you for all your answers that you gave me. I would like to thank you for all your explanations about the issues that I knew very little before I met you today. I wish you all the best. I wish you success in your future work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this brings my cross-examination to an end. I would like to thank you for your assistance as well as all the other staff that has been working in the courtroom in the course of today's examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Elderkin, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions, yes. I don't know how you would wish to handle it, whether we should break a few minutes early or try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your estimation, how many minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Around five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think then we should try to do it before the break because we -- before we finish for today, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, in an answer to Judge Flugge when you were describing the difference between categorising remains as bodies or body parts, you said the difference was semantic. Can you explain further what you mean by that semantic difference?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The impossibility lies in how would you calculate an exact percentage to -- for a body to be a body, or a body not to be a body. So even more beyond semantic, meaning semantic would be that I call a body part where somebody else may say, No it is a body. And it is almost philosophical. Another layer to add to it would be beyond semantics, beyond what I call this or what do you call this? I mean, put a -- a cutting point, this is a body part and this is a body. As I said, this was a permanent -- almost a permanent debate. In some cases, it changed -- a body part would come out from the field a body part and then you give it to the mortuary and become a body, for example, because a pathologist may think that that is a body and not a body part. I would say it's almost an unsolvable problem. You can see that body part is a body part because a pice of somebody. Because then when this somebody is not a piece? If I may explain it in that way. So I would say that yes there have been various or different arguments from different people to call this that or something else, but the essence of what you looking at doesn't really change. I don't know whether I'm explaining because it's very philosophical, but I don't know if I'm explaining it correctly. Are you satisfied with the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied and I would follow up with a further question on the same issue. For the purposes of your work, and in particular for the calculation of minimum number of individuals, does the categorisation of remains as body or body part have any consequence in that calculation?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I mean, none whatsoever. Do remember that these charting with number 1 or 0 for present or absent happened on every thing that was collected from the grave; from a complete body, that would be 1, 1, 1 all over the place; or a piece of a body, that would be 1, 0, 0, 1, and so forth. So no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, you used a hypothetical example when you were describing how -- the example of a soil sample present in secondary graves could show a link to a primary grave. All that was just a hypothetical, but it seemed to me possible that, for example, you might have several primary graves containing similar soil. So are there other ways in which links between primary and secondary graves could be identified and were identified in the Srebrenica graves others than soil samples?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, the information I was privy to obviously used a number of lines of evidence to do that. One was soil, the other one was pollen, the other one were artefacts; for example, textiles that have been found part in one grave and part in the other one, and they would match, you see it's the same piece of cloth. If I'm not mistaken, shell casings demonstrated pretty much that all these casings had been fired by the same weapon and were found in the primary as well as the secondary sites. All possible, I mean, links were established, it was not only soil and pollen. That is quite strong, I have to say, because it's not just solely by looking at the soil. It's something very microscopic and detailed. But, yes, we had many lines of evidence that pointed to those links.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if DNA connections could be used as a way to link primary and secondary graves, for example, if bones from one individual identified through DNA analysis were to be found in two different sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean nowadays, move definitely. Nowadays you would use, I mean, DNA to reassociate parts, and if, as you explaining me, say the arm of somebody would be broken into five pieces and be in five different places, you would be able to use DNA to do a bone-to-bone matching and link all those pieces and would be yet another line of evidence to show that the arm ended up inside 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and are all part of the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You also spoke on cross-examination about one or more occasions where you had to leave an exhumation site because there was some danger from the local population. Do you remember which site that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, from the occasions I remember, back in 1996 was at site of Lazete. Obviously in 1997 happened again, but it has nothing to do with this case. In Brcko happened the same thing. But 1996, I think at least the one time I recall because actually we got stuck in the confrontation was coming out of Lazete, that we have to really leave as we were. I mean, and actually we could not cross the inter-entity boundary line because we got pretty much stuck on the Republika Srpska side and there was a confrontation with local population and the soldiers that were giving us protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar you are with the other local place names, but is the Lazete site you mention the one by an elevated railway line at a place called Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard from other witnesses and reports about DNA testing being used to identify many thousands of Srebrenica victims. Given the unique nature of each individual's DNA, does your process of MNI calculation serve any additional process when dealing with these cases involving victims in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no objections to the witness answering all these questions but I should like to accentuate that this was not the subject of either the cross-examination or of his expertise, this particular issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I hope I was clear in my question as to be asking the witness to explain exactly the area of his expertise which is the purpose of the MNI calculation in view of where we are today, where DNA information is available. I'm not asking him as a DNA expert but as somebody who handles this anthropological question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was my understanding of your question as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is likely that with further identifications, the MNI will change, but my prediction for that matter is that the MNI or the number will increase because as I said before, the minimal number is really a very conservative estimate. If you are able now to reassociate body parts many of which were not used for the MNI, because you have to be very consistent with the type of bone you're using, it is highly likely the number will go up. That's a commonsensical conclusion from this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is there a separate purpose to the MNI calculation from the purpose for which the DNA identification process is used? Does it add anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I mean, obviously a DNA adds something but let's put things into context again. When these calculations were done, there was no DNA in the way we know it now, okay? So you got a very fair and conservative estimate regarding how many people would be represented by these remains. Now we do have DNA. What DNA will allow us to do is to increase the number of people that fell through the cracks, so to speak, in these estimation of the minimal number of individuals. DNA would allow us to do something that we should call a maximum number of individuals, meaning you'll be able to reassociate all those parts that were not, I mean, counted because they were not consistent with the type of bone we were looking at. So, yes, there is a point. I mean, it's a major technology breakthrough that has to be used, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So there is clearly, as you observe, an additional purpose because for DNA work that's being done now but looking at it in the reverse, does there remain a purpose for the MNI work that you have done? If the same hypothetical occurred now that you were called to investigate a mass grave, would MNI serve any purpose given the availability of DNA techniques?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to answer you now, in very clear terms. Well, of course DNA is available, if you can pay for it. So I'm being very blunt here because then you're drawing on my expertise beyond this Tribunal. The MNI is a basic thing to lead further approaches such as DNA. DNA is yet an accessory technique, as many others, to prove or disprove something, but you have to start from somewhere, to validate that somewhere. Your MNI is a somewhere where you start from. What DNA will do to your MNI is first it will confirm your MNI and then it will increase it because you will be using also other parts that were not as part of your original calculation of MNI. But certainly, it's like saying to an anthropologist whether bones would be of any use because we have DNA now and certainly that's not the issue. I mean, DNA contributes and gives you a piece of the puzzle, so to speak, but all these processes are totally valid and would have been done in the same way now, having DNA. A lot of this is the most basic groundwork that any anthropological investigation has to do, be it the Balkans, be in Peru, in the Congo, whatever. And the issue, of course, understanding as well the issue of DNA is an issue of resources. I mean there is a number of techniques available but I would not say that all countries have access to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Presiding Judge. I said that the DNA was not the subject of either the examination or of this expertise. I should now like to ask is the OTP contesting the minimum number as such? Does this call in question the expertise of this witness and his final report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we are not challenging our own witness. We are presenting his evidence as called here live today and in his reports and prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are there any more questions, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours and thank you very much for your indulgence for those extra minutes and thank you to the interpretation staff and other staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Baraybar, thank you very much for all the answers you were able to give us and, indeed, I would join Mr. Tolimir, we have learned a lot, and now you are free to return to your normal activities. Thank you again for your attendance here and your expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, Mr. McCloskey, is there another witness available for half an hour today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. President. I think it would be better if we just started with Mr. Janc in the afternoon tomorrow as opposed to trying to get something done today when I think it would be better to wait if we could. It's not much time left really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. I would agree. If there are no other matters to discuss today, then we have to adjourn and resume tomorrow quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of November, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.00 p.m.,
